hints: Look carefully at the tick pattern for ciliated cells. Which three parts have them and which one part has none at all?
Remember what cleans air (mucus from goblet cells plus sweeping by cilia) and what gas exchange needs (very thin walls with no muscle to get in the way).
walkthrough:
**Spot the cleaning team**

Think of cleaning as a mucus escalator. Goblet cells make sticky mucus to trap dust and microbes, and ciliated cells beat to sweep it up and out.

Look at the table: trachea and bronchus have both ticks, so they definitely clean. Bronchiole has ciliated cells (tick) even though it has no goblet cells, so it can still keep sweeping mucus along.

**Spot the gas exchange surface**

Gas exchange needs a super thin, delicate surface with a rich blood supply and no thick muscle layer. Smooth muscle would make the wall too thick.

Only the alveoli have crosses (X) for all three cell types, meaning no cilia, no goblet cells and no smooth muscle. That gives the thinnest possible wall for diffusion.

**Match to the options**

Cleaning needs cilia, so trachea, bronchus and bronchiole. Gas exchange needs no muscle and thin walls, so alveoli only.

That combination is exactly option D.

options.A: Back to front. Alveoli have no cilia so cannot clean, and trachea and bronchus are too thick walled for gas exchange.
options.B: Partly right about trachea and bronchus cleaning, but it wrongly leaves out the bronchiole which has cilia, and bronchioles do not carry out gas exchange.
options.C: Right that trachea and bronchus clean, but it misses the bronchiole for cleaning and wrongly adds the bronchiole to gas exchange.
options.D: Correct. Trachea, bronchus and bronchiole all have ciliated cells to move mucus and clean air, while only alveoli lack all three cell types giving thin walls for gas exchange.
